State v. Aho
facts: Petitioner Fonua Aho was convicted of child molestation and rape in the Superior Court for King County. Aho subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that convicting him for violating §9A.44.083 violated the prohibition against ex post facto laws in both the United States Constitution (Article 1 §10) and the Washington State Constitution (Article 1 §23) as he had been convicted on the basis of conduct spanning an eight-year period from 1987 through 1995 and §9A.44.083 had not taken effect until 1988. Thus, as the jury had not been asked to identify precisely when the acts giving rise to the conviction had occurred, Aho claimed that the possibility that he had been convicted for acts that preceded the effective date of the relevant statute violated his due process rights. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Aho's conviction, holding that §9A.44.083 merely recodified the prohibition against conduct already prohibited by its predecessor statute. Aho appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Aho's conviction constitute an ex post facto application of the law?
conclusions: Justice Madsen's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed Aho's conviction, concluding that §9A.44.083 did not simply recodify the same offense already prohibited by the indecent liberties statute that preceded it as it had different age and age differential elements. Therefore, as §9A.44.083 represented a new statute rather than a recodification and could not be applied to conduct preceding its 1988 effective date, convicting Aho without requiring that the jury specify the date on which the acts giving rise to his conviction occurred violated Aho's right to due process.

Enterprise Leasing , d/b/a Enterprise Rent-A-Car, Petitioner, v. City of Tacoma, Finance Department, Respondent
facts: Petitioner Enterprise Leasing filed suit in the Superior Court for Pierce County seeking a declaratory judgment that the city of Tacoma's attempt to assess its income at the higher local business and occupation tax rate applied to services rather than the local business and occupation tax rate applied to retail sales was invalid insofar as it was inconsistent with the definitions of retail sales and services established by state law. The Superior Court for Pierce County granted summary judgment to Enterprise Leasing and ordered the company's income to be assessed at the lower retail sales rate. On appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's decision, holding that the city of Tacoma was not prohibited from defining retail sales differently than the state. Enterprise Leasing appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May local governments define the term "retail sales" differently than the state for the purposes of assessing business and occupation taxes?
conclusions: Justice Smith's opinion for a unanimous Court ruled that local governments may generally define taxation categories as they see fit unless expressly constrained by a statute or constitutional provision. Thus, as Washington Revised Code §35.21.710, in defining "retail sales" for state purposes, did not expressly state that it was exclusive and superseded other definitions of "retail sales," the city of Tacoma was free to define the term in other ways.

title: Frederick L. Jones, Sr., Respondent, v. Sisters of Providence in Washington, a Washington corporation d/b/a Providence Medical Center and Providence Family Medical Center, Defendant, Susan Lo, M.D., and Richard G. Foutch, M.D., Petitioners
State v. Baity
facts: Respondent Michael Baity was charged with driving under the influence after police utilized a 12-step drug recognition expert protocol to determine that Baity had been driving while under the influence of marijuana. At trial in the Superior Court for Pierce County, Baity successfully sought to suppress testimony from the drug recognition expert after the trial court concluded that the protocol employed lacked scientific validity and dismissed the charges. The state of Washington appealed the trial court's decision to exclude the expert testimony to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the 12-step protocol employed by drug recognition experts meet the criteria established in Frye v. United States for determining whether evidence based upon novel scientific is admissible?
conclusions: Justice Talmadge's opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the trial court's decision regarding the admissibility of testimony by drug recognition experts, concluding that the protocol satisfied the criteria delineated in Frye insofar as it had attained general acceptance in the relevant scientific community and a properly qualified expert could utilize the protocol to form an opinion about the presence or absence of certain categories of drugs in a defendant's system.
